analysis.title: AI Is Everywhere But In The Business Cycle
key_insights: AI changes how the economy operates but does not rise to a level that reshapes the current US business cycle for spending and hiring, except among Asian exporters.
Recession is far off. Nominal GDP is running near 7% SAAR with the 10Y at 5% and the funds rate at 3.88%. The author guesses 2029 as the recession year.

The Fed believes only a modest course correction is needed to return inflation to target and will lag current events. TS Lombard expects higher inflation and higher interest rates than the Fed and market price in.
Recession needs rates pulled well ahead of nominal growth and a meaningful fiscal tightening through spending cuts or tax hikes. Neither condition is present.

Census classifies AI data plants as office buildings. Real office construction spending rose $28bn Y/Y for the 12 months ending August, down from a peak of $37bn Y/Y in the 12 months ending last November. Private power construction is up $5.4bn.

Office construction was increasing around $60bn a year in the late 1990s. Current AI-related construction does not offset the $188bn decline in manufacturing construction or the $219bn decline in total private nonresidential construction.
Given a lead/lag of about two years between profits and construction, the author expects private nonresidential construction to pick up in the next year or two.

Real capital spending as a share of real final sales has risen from 10% after the 2008-09 recession to 14.7%, with 12.5% as the midpoint in 2019. Software is now 4% of real final sales, up from 1.4% in 2012. This is a shift in what businesses buy more than a jump in total spending.

Business capex ex structures contributed 1.075% to real GDP growth in Q2 (4Q moving average), above the long-run median. The late 1990s median contribution was 1.15%. Real GDP growth is slowing, so the AI capex multiplier is smaller than advertised.
The economy is in year one of recovery after a non-recession recession in 2025, so other contributors to GDP growth are expected to accelerate in the year ahead.
The AI buildout is being imported. There is no surge in orders or shipments of computers and electronic products relative to the non-defense total, and imports of advanced technology have surged.

Employment shows no AI boom. Computer services employment has fallen since 2022, and nonresidential construction employment has kept pace with total employment. An AI bust is therefore unlikely to create a surge in unemployment.
Payroll tends to follow profits, so there is guarded optimism that hiring by AI-related firms increases next year.

AI deflation is limited. Food at home, energy, housing and medical services are near 70% of CPI, while legal and financial services are 0.4%. Materials and components PPI for manufacturing is inflating faster than construction materials.
AI-related borrowers now pay spreads that better reflect risk. If every AI bond defaulted, the amount outstanding would still be small next to the 2007 mortgage market.

The main risk is capital import. Net investment running above net domestic saving pushes real yields up, with the Fed balance sheet normally acting as ballast. With Warsh backing away from that role, real yields are rising. A weaker dollar would raise inflation and undercut the Fed's view that inflation trends lower next year.
Business net investment is running at 3% of GDP, the median since 2003. AI is borrowing more but total net investment shows no surge, and the author doubts AI is crowding out other borrowers.

Boom/bust potential sits in the equity market more than in real spending flows. Equities are repricing to a normalized forward P/E for AI firms, with 15 too low and 50 too high. The author calls this a functioning market, not a bust. If equities crashed the Fed would ease.
The author says a 50bp hike in December, to make up for the skip this week, would signal the Fed shifting to a more aggressive stance.

sector_views.rationale: AI changes how the economy operates but does not drive the business cycle. Valuation is repricing to a normalized forward P/E between 15 and 50, which the author calls a functioning market.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Strong nominal growth with cheap and plentiful money means recession is not imminent.
Yield sits below nominal growth, which is not the restrictive setup that precedes a recession.
Policy rate is well below nominal GDP growth, so policy is not restrictive.

risk_factors: The rest of the world forces the US to pay much higher real rates for importing capital, which could bring recession sooner.
Net investment above net domestic saving raises real yields, especially with the Fed balance sheet no longer acting as ballast.
A falling dollar raises inflation and undercuts the Fed's expectation of lower inflation next year.
The Fed lags inflation and market pricing of lower inflation proves wrong.
Higher-skilled income trajectories fall and the effect trickles down to gig workers.
An AI equity repricing hits asset prices, although the author expects the Fed to ease in a crash.
charts_described: Chart 1 plots Y/Y $bn increase in real private nonresidential construction, with office construction (AI plants) showing only a blip.
Chart 3 shows business capex ex structures adding to real GDP growth but not at record levels.
Chart 9 shows net investment relative to net saving and the 10-year TIPS yield, with real yields rising when the Fed stops buying.
vol_and_positioning: Signs of non-dollar investor disquiet abound, and weaker holders of US dollar assets may demand greater compensation.

tension_points.bull_case: AI-related firms make money, money is cheap and plentiful, nominal GDP runs near 7%, and the Fed would ease if equities crashed. A near-term reversal in AI spending would not reverse the economy.
tension_points.bear_case: AI borrowing and government borrowing push net investment above net domestic saving, raising real yields. A weaker dollar would raise inflation and the Fed lags, so rates could eventually rise well ahead of nominal growth.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A 50bp Fed hike in December would signal the Fed shifting to a more aggressive stance, and real yields rising to contractionary levels on a global capital strike would bring recession sooner than 2029.

theme_stances.key_argument: AI spending and hiring are too small to reshape the current US business cycle, and an AI bust would not push the economy into recession.
theme_stances.evidence: AI is transformative to how we operate but not to the business cycle

theme_stances.key_argument: The Fed believes a modest course correction returns inflation to target, and TS Lombard expects higher inflation and rates than the market prices.
theme_stances.evidence: the Fed's perception, duly priced in by the market, will be proven very wrong
